Well, doctor, what brings me in is that I keep hearing these very, very clear voices in my apartment. I've lived in that apartment for over twenty years, right after I finished my degree, and it has these gorgeous pre-war details, you know? The crown molding is just exquisite, though the radiator clanks terribly in the winter. 

But anyway, yes, the voices. And it's not just at home, it happens in empty museum rooms too. I'll be standing there, and I hear these women whispering from right behind the walls, telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. Which is interesting, because archiving is such a meticulous process, really. I used to organize all my family's photo albums. My grandmother had these wonderful sepia portraits from the twenties, back when people actually dressed up to get their picture taken. People don't dress up anymore, do they? You go to the theater or the museum now and people are just wearing jeans and tennis shoes. It's a real shame. 

But yes... the women whispering behind the walls about the photographs. They're just getting very hard to ignore.

Oh, my mood... well, on those days, I feel absolutely radiant. Like I've been chosen for something magnificent, you know? "Radiant" is such a wonderful word. It makes me think of radium. Well, depressed... yes, I suppose you could say that. There are these long, long stretches where I just sit at my kitchen table. I have these little terracotta pots of herbs on the windowsill—basil, thyme, a lovely rosemary bush. But during those times, I just sit there and watch them dry out. The ancient Romans used it for everything, even their plumbing pipes. I read somewhere that the Roman aqueducts were an absolute marvel of engineering. They moved water across entire valleys using just gravity. Gravity is a strange thing to think about. It holds us down, but sometimes I feel like I'm floating away. 

But yes, I just sit at the table. People call, but I don't call them back. Friends will invite me out—Susan will say, "Let's go to a gallery opening" or "There's a wonderful string quartet playing at the conservatory." And I just... I don't care. I have no interest at all. Which is so unlike me, because I adore chamber music. A good cello can sound exactly like a human voice crying. Yo-Yo Ma plays a Stradivarius cello from 1712, I believe. The craftsmanship of those old Italian instruments... they say the secret was in the varnish, or maybe the density of the wood because of a mini ice age in Europe at the time. An ice age! Imagine the Thames freezing over so solid they held frost fairs on it. They would roast whole oxen right there on the ice. But no, I don't go to the concerts. I just sit by the dry herbs.

Oh, the whispers... yes, they don't just go away because I'm sitting there feeling low. There was a period of several weeks, actually, when I wasn't feeling radiant or energized at all. Just completely drained. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment the whole time. The acoustics in my building are very particular. It's a pre-war building, you see, built in 1928. They used real lath and plaster back then, not that flimsy drywall they put up today. Plastering is really a lost art. I watched a fascinating program on public television about how they used to mix horsehair into the wet plaster to bind it together and keep it from cracking. Imagine that, horsehair right inside your walls! Horses are such magnificent, sensitive creatures. My grandfather had a farm in upstate New York with two beautiful Clydesdales. Their hooves were the size of dinner plates, and they had those lovely white feathers around their ankles. I used to feed them sugar cubes right out of my palm. You have to keep your hand perfectly flat so they don't nip your fingers. 

But yes, I'd be sitting there feeling just dreadful, hearing those women whispering, and I was absolutely convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone. My phone is an original heavy black Bakelite rotary model. Bakelite was the very first synthetic plastic, invented by a Belgian chemist. It's practically indestructible. They used to make the most gorgeous jewelry out of it in the 1920s and 30s—chunky Art Deco bangles in cherry red and butterscotch yellow. Art Deco is simply my favorite design period. The Chrysler Building is the absolute pinnacle of it, don't you think? Those stainless steel arches catching the sun like a crown. It used to be the tallest building in the world, though only for about a year before the Empire State Building surpassed it. It's all just a race to the top, isn't it? But yes, they were definitely listening in on that Bakelite phone, even when I didn't have the energy to pick it up.

The crown molding is just exquisite, though the radiator clanks terribly in the winter. \n\nBut anyway, yes, the voices. And it's not just at home, it happens in empty museum rooms too. I'll be standing there, and I hear these women whispering from right behind the walls, telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. Which is interesting, because archiving is such a meticulous process, really. I used to organize all my family's photo albums. My grandmother had these wonderful sepia portraits from the twenties, back when people actually dressed up to get their picture taken. People don't dress up anymore, do they? You go to the theater or the museum now and people are just wearing jeans and tennis shoes. It's a real shame. \n\nBut yes... the women whispering behind the walls about the photographs. They're just getting very hard to ignore.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been hearing these voices? When did they first start?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think... it's been about eight months now. Yes, eight months of those whispers, and just this absolute certainty that people are watching my archive. Watching me sort through it. It started right around the time I was trying to reorganize my winter coats, actually. I have this beautiful wool houndstooth coat that I bought in London years ago. Oh, the shopping in London back then was just marvelous. You could find the most incredible tailoring. I remember walking down Oxford Street and stopping in for tea at this little place that served the most delicate scones with clotted cream. You just can't find proper clotted cream here, can you? It's always too thin or too sweet. I tried making it myself once, but the milk wasn't right. You need unpasteurized milk, I think. But anyway, yes, it's been about eight months since they started telling me about the photographs.\n\nDoctor: Over these past eight months, have there been times when you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or felt like you could accomplish a lot more than you usually do?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Sometimes I just have so much energy I don't even know what to do with it. There are these nights where I'll start out labeling photographs for the archive, and then suddenly I'm rewriting donor letters, and then I'm reorganizing entire boxes of theater programs without even sitting down once. My body just feels like it has a motor running through it, you know? It's actually how I managed to get through all those Playbills from the 1980s. I have quite the collection. I used to go to Broadway shows all the time with my friend Susan. Susan had this incredible knack for getting rush tickets. We saw Cats three times, if you can believe it. The costumes were just magnificent. I always thought I would have liked to design costumes, working with all those different fabrics—velvets and silks and brocades. Did you know that real silk is spun by caterpillars? It's fascinating. I read a whole book about the Silk Road once. But yes, those nights with the motor running, I just keep moving and moving from one project to the next.\n\nDoctor: During those nights when you have all that energy and keep moving from project to project, how is your mood? Do you feel particularly happy, excited, or on top of the world—or does your mood feel more normal, or perhaps irritable or down?\n\nPatient: Oh, my mood... well, on those days, I feel absolutely radiant. Like I've been chosen for something magnificent, you know? \"Radiant\" is such a wonderful word. It makes me think of radium. Did you know they used to paint watch dials with radium so they would glow in the dark? The poor girls who painted them, the Radium Girls, they would lick their brushes to get a fine point. Just a terrible tragedy. I used to have a beautiful vintage watch with a mother-of-pearl face, though it wasn't radium, thank goodness. My father bought it for me in Switzerland. Switzerland is breathtaking in the spring. The Alps just pierce the sky, and the air is so crisp. I always wanted to go back and take the Glacier Express train. \n\nBut yes, radiant and chosen. That's exactly how I feel. Until someone interrupts me, that is. If anyone questions my plan for the archive, or tells me I need to slow down and get some sleep? Oh, I become furious. Just livid! It feels exactly like they are trying to erase me. Erase my work, erase my very existence. Like an eraser on a chalkboard. I used to love the smell of chalk dust in elementary school... the teacher would ask me to take the erasers outside and clap them together against the brick wall. Such a satisfying puff of white dust. But yes, it's infuriating when they try to erase me like that.\n\nDoctor: Besides these times when you feel radiant and energetic with the voices, have you had extended periods—lasting weeks or longer—where you felt depressed, sad, or hopeless, even if the voices weren't happening or seemed quieter?\n\nPatient: Well, depressed... yes, I suppose you could say that. There are these long, long stretches where I just sit at my kitchen table. I have these little terracotta pots of herbs on the windowsill—basil, thyme, a lovely rosemary bush. But during those times, I just sit there and watch them dry out. I don't water them, I don't pinch off the dead leaves. I just sit. Terracotta is such a fascinating material, isn't it? \"Baked earth\" in Italian. The ancient Romans used it for everything, even their plumbing pipes. I read somewhere that the Roman aqueducts were an absolute marvel of engineering. They moved water across entire valleys using just gravity. Gravity is a strange thing to think about. It holds us down, but sometimes I feel like I'm floating away. \n\nBut yes, I just sit at the table. People call, but I don't call them back. Friends will invite me out—Susan will say, \"Let's go to a gallery opening\" or \"There's a wonderful string quartet playing at the conservatory.\" And I just... I don't care. I have no interest at all. Which is so unlike me, because I adore chamber music. A good cello can sound exactly like a human voice crying. Yo-Yo Ma plays a Stradivarius cello from 1712, I believe. The craftsmanship of those old Italian instruments... they say the secret was in the varnish, or maybe the density of the wood because of a mini ice age in Europe at the time. An ice age! Imagine the Thames freezing over so solid they held frost fairs on it. They would roast whole oxen right there on the ice. But no, I don't go to the concerts. I just sit by the dry herbs.\n\nDoctor: During those long stretches when you're sitting by the kitchen table feeling depressed and not interested in anything—when your mood is low like that—are you still hearing the voices from the women whispering about the photographs, or do the voices go away during those periods?\n\nPatient: Oh, the whispers... yes, they don't just go away because I'm sitting there feeling low. There was a period of several weeks, actually, when I wasn't feeling radiant or energized at all. Just completely drained. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment the whole time. The acoustics in my building are very particular. It's a pre-war building, you see, built in 1928. They used real lath and plaster back then, not that flimsy drywall they put up today. Plastering is really a lost art. I watched a fascinating program on public television about how they used to mix horsehair into the wet plaster to bind it together and keep it from cracking. Imagine that, horsehair right inside your walls! Horses are such magnificent, sensitive creatures. My grandfather had a farm in upstate New York with two beautiful Clydesdales. Their hooves were the size of dinner plates, and they had those lovely white feathers around their ankles. I used to feed them sugar cubes right out of my palm. You have to keep your hand perfectly flat so they don't nip your fingers. \n\nBut yes, I'd be sitting there feeling just dreadful, hearing those women whispering, and I was absolutely convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone. My phone is an original heavy black Bakelite rotary model. Bakelite was the very first synthetic plastic, invented by a Belgian chemist. It's practically indestructible. They used to make the most gorgeous jewelry out of it in the 1920s and 30s—chunky Art Deco bangles in cherry red and butterscotch yellow. Art Deco is simply my favorite design period. The Chrysler Building is the absolute pinnacle of it, don't you think? Those stainless steel arches catching the sun like a crown. It used to be the tallest building in the world, though only for about a year before the Empire State Building surpassed it. It's all just a race to the top, isn't it? But yes, they were definitely listening in on that Bakelite phone, even when I didn't have the energy to pick it up.\n\nDoctor: When you're feeling your normal baseline mood—not radiant and energized, and not sitting at the kitchen table feeling drained—do you still hear those women's voices whispering about the photographs, or do they only happen during those extreme mood states?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I've told you... even when I'm just feeling, you know, regular. Neither here nor there. Not radiant, not drained. There was that period of several weeks, just recently, where I wasn't especially energized or grand at all. Just my normal self. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment. The women talking about the photographs. And I remained absolutely convinced that the arts people were monitoring my phone. \n\nPhotography is such a delicate process, especially the old methods. Have you ever seen a daguerreotype? They are just magical. They're on silver-plated copper, and you have to tilt them just right in the light to see the image, otherwise it just looks like a mirror. A mirror into the past! The chemicals they used were so dangerous, though. Mercury vapor. Mad as a hatter, they say, because hat makers used mercury too. Lewis Carroll knew what he was doing when he wrote the Mad Hatter. Alice in Wonderland is full of such brilliant mathematical jokes because Carroll was actually a mathematician at Oxford. Charles Dodgson was his real name. Oxford is a place I've always wanted to see—the dreaming spires, they call it. The architecture is just... well, it's monumental. But yes, the whispers are there even when my mood is just fine.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. They are very real. Oh, yes. Even when I'm just going about my normal day, making a cup of tea or reading the paper, I keep hearing these clear voices in my apartment. Well, they definitely aren't my own thoughts. No, they're coming from outside. Like I said, I keep hearing these clear voices in my apartment, like women whispering right from behind the walls, telling me which photographs belong in the archive. And sometimes I hear them when I'm out, too, in empty museum rooms.

Yes, eight months of those whispers, and just this absolute certainty that people are watching my archive. Watching me sort through it. It started right around the time I was trying to reorganize my winter coats, actually. I have this beautiful wool houndstooth coat that I bought in London years ago. Oh, the shopping in London back then was just marvelous. You could find the most incredible tailoring. I remember walking down Oxford Street and stopping in for tea at this little place that served the most delicate scones with clotted cream. You just can't find proper clotted cream here, can you? It's always too thin or too sweet. I tried making it myself once, but the milk wasn't right. You need unpasteurized milk, I think. But anyway, yes, it's been about eight months since they started telling me about the photographs.\n\nDoctor: Over these past eight months, have there been times when you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or felt like you could accomplish a lot more than you usually do?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Sometimes I just have so much energy I don't even know what to do with it. There are these nights where I'll start out labeling photographs for the archive, and then suddenly I'm rewriting donor letters, and then I'm reorganizing entire boxes of theater programs without even sitting down once. My body just feels like it has a motor running through it, you know? It's actually how I managed to get through all those Playbills from the 1980s. I have quite the collection. I used to go to Broadway shows all the time with my friend Susan. Susan had this incredible knack for getting rush tickets. We saw Cats three times, if you can believe it. The costumes were just magnificent. I always thought I would have liked to design costumes, working with all those different fabrics—velvets and silks and brocades. Did you know that real silk is spun by caterpillars? It's fascinating. I read a whole book about the Silk Road once. But yes, those nights with the motor running, I just keep moving and moving from one project to the next.\n\nDoctor: During those nights when you have all that energy and keep moving from project to project, how is your mood? Do you feel particularly happy, excited, or on top of the world—or does your mood feel more normal, or perhaps irritable or down?\n\nPatient: Oh, my mood... well, on those days, I feel absolutely radiant. Like I've been chosen for something magnificent, you know? \"Radiant\" is such a wonderful word. It makes me think of radium. Did you know they used to paint watch dials with radium so they would glow in the dark? The poor girls who painted them, the Radium Girls, they would lick their brushes to get a fine point. Just a terrible tragedy. I used to have a beautiful vintage watch with a mother-of-pearl face, though it wasn't radium, thank goodness. My father bought it for me in Switzerland. Switzerland is breathtaking in the spring. The Alps just pierce the sky, and the air is so crisp. I always wanted to go back and take the Glacier Express train. \n\nBut yes, radiant and chosen. That's exactly how I feel. Until someone interrupts me, that is. If anyone questions my plan for the archive, or tells me I need to slow down and get some sleep? Oh, I become furious. Just livid! It feels exactly like they are trying to erase me. Erase my work, erase my very existence. Like an eraser on a chalkboard. I used to love the smell of chalk dust in elementary school... the teacher would ask me to take the erasers outside and clap them together against the brick wall. Such a satisfying puff of white dust. But yes, it's infuriating when they try to erase me like that.\n\nDoctor: Besides these times when you feel radiant and energetic with the voices, have you had extended periods—lasting weeks or longer—where you felt depressed, sad, or hopeless, even if the voices weren't happening or seemed quieter?\n\nPatient: Well, depressed... yes, I suppose you could say that. But during those times, I just sit there and watch them dry out. I don't water them, I don't pinch off the dead leaves. I just sit. Terracotta is such a fascinating material, isn't it? \"Baked earth\" in Italian. The ancient Romans used it for everything, even their plumbing pipes. I read somewhere that the Roman aqueducts were an absolute marvel of engineering. They moved water across entire valleys using just gravity. Gravity is a strange thing to think about. It holds us down, but sometimes I feel like I'm floating away. \n\nBut yes, I just sit at the table. People call, but I don't call them back. There was a period of several weeks, actually, when I wasn't feeling radiant or energized at all. Just completely drained. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment the whole time. The acoustics in my building are very particular. It's a pre-war building, you see, built in 1928. They used real lath and plaster back then, not that flimsy drywall they put up today. Plastering is really a lost art. I watched a fascinating program on public television about how they used to mix horsehair into the wet plaster to bind it together and keep it from cracking. Imagine that, horsehair right inside your walls! Horses are such magnificent, sensitive creatures. My grandfather had a farm in upstate New York with two beautiful Clydesdales. They used to make the most gorgeous jewelry out of it in the 1920s and 30s—chunky Art Deco bangles in cherry red and butterscotch yellow. Art Deco is simply my favorite design period. The Chrysler Building is the absolute pinnacle of it, don't you think? Those stainless steel arches catching the sun like a crown. Yes, oh absolutely. It was a period of several weeks, definitely longer than two. During that whole stretch, I wasn't especially energized or grand at all. Just... regular, like I said. Friends will invite me out—Susan will say, \"Let's go to a gallery opening\" or \"There's a wonderful string quartet playing at the conservatory.\" And I just... I don't care. I have no interest at all. Which is so unlike me, because I adore chamber music. A good cello can sound exactly like a human voice crying. Yo-Yo Ma plays a Stradivarius cello from 1712, I believe. The craftsmanship of those old Italian instruments... they say the secret was in the varnish, or maybe the density of the wood because of a mini ice age in Europe at the time. An ice age! Imagine the Thames freezing over so solid they held frost fairs on it. They would roast whole oxen right there on the ice. But no, I don't go to the concerts. I just sit by the dry herbs.\n\nDoctor: During those long stretches when you're sitting by the kitchen table feeling depressed and not interested in anything—when your mood is low like that—are you still hearing the voices from the women whispering about the photographs, or do the voices go away during those periods?\n\nPatient: Oh, the whispers... yes, they don't just go away because I'm sitting there feeling low. There was a period of several weeks, actually, when I wasn't feeling radiant or energized at all. Just completely drained. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment the whole time. The acoustics in my building are very particular. It's a pre-war building, you see, built in 1928. They used real lath and plaster back then, not that flimsy drywall they put up today. Plastering is really a lost art. I watched a fascinating program on public television about how they used to mix horsehair into the wet plaster to bind it together and keep it from cracking. Imagine that, horsehair right inside your walls! Horses are such magnificent, sensitive creatures. My grandfather had a farm in upstate New York with two beautiful Clydesdales. Their hooves were the size of dinner plates, and they had those lovely white feathers around their ankles. I used to feed them sugar cubes right out of my palm. You have to keep your hand perfectly flat so they don't nip your fingers. \n\nBut yes, I'd be sitting there feeling just dreadful, hearing those women whispering, and I was absolutely convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone. My phone is an original heavy black Bakelite rotary model. Bakelite was the very first synthetic plastic, invented by a Belgian chemist. It's practically indestructible. They used to make the most gorgeous jewelry out of it in the 1920s and 30s—chunky Art Deco bangles in cherry red and butterscotch yellow. Art Deco is simply my favorite design period. The Chrysler Building is the absolute pinnacle of it, don't you think? Those stainless steel arches catching the sun like a crown. It used to be the tallest building in the world, though only for about a year before the Empire State Building surpassed it. It's all just a race to the top, isn't it? But yes, they were definitely listening in on that Bakelite phone, even when I didn't have the energy to pick it up.\n\nDoctor: When you're feeling your normal baseline mood—not radiant and energized, and not sitting at the kitchen table feeling drained—do you still hear those women's voices whispering about the photographs, or do they only happen during those extreme mood states?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I've told you... even when I'm just feeling, you know, regular. Alice in Wonderland is full of such brilliant mathematical jokes because Carroll was actually a mathematician at Oxford. Charles Dodgson was his real name. Oxford is a place I've always wanted to see—the dreaming spires, they call it. The architecture is just... well, it's monumental. Well, I would have said yes with absolute certainty. I still say yes with absolute certainty. I mean, I am completely convinced the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. They know my Caribbean archive will change how the galleries tell the truth, and no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise. Henry Fonda was brilliant in that movie. He had such a calm demeanor. My father loved Henry Fonda. We used to watch old black-and-white movies on Sunday afternoons. They had this big, heavy Zenith television set in a wooden cabinet. It took a full minute just to warm up the tubes before the picture would appear. Vacuum tubes! Now people walk around with tiny computers in their pockets, pretending they're just phones. But they aren't just phones, are they? They're tracking devices. Everyone willingly carrying around a little tracking device. It's exactly like George Orwell predicted in 1984, only we bought the screens ourselves. Big Brother doesn't even have to force us. 

But yes, doctor, I was and still am completely certain about the arts people monitoring my phone. There's no doubt in my mind at all.

Plastering is really a lost art. I watched a fascinating program on public television about how they used to mix horsehair into the wet plaster to bind it together and keep it from cracking. Yes, exactly. Like I was saying before, there was a period of several weeks when I wasn't having any of those radiant nights. Well, I always feel like my thinking is perfectly logical, but I suppose it doesn't always come out that way to other people, even when my mood is just regular. Like, my cousin will call and ask me a very simple question, just about a utility bill or an upcoming appointment, and I try to answer her. But I'll start explaining the archive grant, and then that leads into the historical Caribbean shipping routes, and then I'll get into talking about my grandmother’s altar, and by the time I finally stop talking, nobody seems to know what I meant at all. She just gets so confused. 

The shipping routes really are fascinating, though. The trade winds just naturally carry the vessels across the Atlantic. The ocean currents are like invisible highways in the water. Water is so incredibly powerful, isn't it? It carves out entire canyons over millions of years. When I was a little girl, I used to love walking along the beach collecting sea glass. You'd find these beautiful, frosted pieces of green and blue glass that used to be medicine bottles or soda bottles. They say it takes decades for the sand and the waves to tumble a sharp piece of broken glass into something that smooth. We used to put them in a clear mason jar on the kitchen windowsill so the morning sun would shine right through them. 

My mother had this gorgeous stained glass lamp in the parlor, too. It was a Tiffany style, with these intricate green dragonflies all around the shade. Dragonflies are actually incredible creatures, you know. They can fly backwards and hover in mid-air like tiny little helicopters. I read once that they catch their prey with almost a ninety-five percent success rate, which is better than lions or sharks or anything else in the animal kingdom. Nature is just perfectly designed that way... 

But I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, my thoughts. Yes, even during those quiet weeks, my cousin would ask about a simple bill and I'd just lose her completely with everything else going on in my head.

No, they're coming from outside. Like I said, I keep hearing these clear voices in my apartment, like women whispering right from behind the walls, telling me which photographs belong in the archive. Climate control is absolutely vital for preserving photographs and paintings. If it gets too humid, you get foxing—those little brown spots on old paper. The largest living organism on earth is actually a fungus in Oregon. A honey fungus, they call it. It covers thousands of acres underground, just this massive network of mycelium. It makes you think about how the old switchboard operators used to be able to just listen in on anyone's conversation if they wanted to. My great-aunt Mildred was a switchboard operator back in the 1940s. She had to sit in this cramped room for hours, just plugging those heavy cords into the giant board, connecting calls all across the city. Well, when they first started eight months ago, my mood was actually just completely regular. There was a period of several weeks right at the beginning when I was not especially energized or grand at all, but I still heard the whispers in the apartment and I remained absolutely convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone.

If you were calling someone with a lot of eights and nines in their number, it took forever! And that cord, it would get so twisted up over time. My mother used to stretch it all the way into the dining room so she could smoke a cigarette and talk to her sister in private. Smoking was everywhere back then. People even smoked on airplanes and in hospitals! Can you imagine? The flight attendants used to walk down the aisles handing out little packets of cigarettes with the airline logo on them. Flying used to be such an elegant experience. People would dress up in their Sunday best just to get on a plane. The stewardesses wore those beautiful tailored uniforms, sometimes designed by famous couturiers like Emilio Pucci. He used such bold, geometric prints and bright colors. Fashion in the sixties was really just a massive explosion of color and freedom after the strictness of the fifties... 

Oh, I'm sorry, I drifted off again. But yes, to answer your question, when it all first began eight months ago, I wasn't energized. It was a stretch of several weeks where I felt completely normal, but the whispers and the phone monitoring were already happening.

I'll be standing there, and I hear these women whispering from right behind the walls, telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. You go to the theater or the museum now and people are just wearing jeans and tennis shoes. It's a real shame. \n\nBut yes... the women whispering behind the walls about the photographs. They're just getting very hard to ignore.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been hearing these voices? When did they first start?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think... it's been about eight months now. Yes, eight months of those whispers, and just this absolute certainty that people are watching my archive. Watching me sort through it. It started right around the time I was trying to reorganize my winter coats, actually. I have this beautiful wool houndstooth coat that I bought in London years ago. Oh, the shopping in London back then was just marvelous. You could find the most incredible tailoring. I remember walking down Oxford Street and stopping in for tea at this little place that served the most delicate scones with clotted cream. You just can't find proper clotted cream here, can you? It's always too thin or too sweet. I tried making it myself once, but the milk wasn't right. You need unpasteurized milk, I think. But anyway, yes, it's been about eight months since they started telling me about the photographs.\n\nDoctor: Over these past eight months, have there been times when you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or felt like you could accomplish a lot more than you usually do?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Sometimes I just have so much energy I don't even know what to do with it. There are these nights where I'll start out labeling photographs for the archive, and then suddenly I'm rewriting donor letters, and then I'm reorganizing entire boxes of theater programs without even sitting down once. My body just feels like it has a motor running through it, you know? It's actually how I managed to get through all those Playbills from the 1980s. I have quite the collection. I used to go to Broadway shows all the time with my friend Susan. Susan had this incredible knack for getting rush tickets. We saw Cats three times, if you can believe it. The costumes were just magnificent. I always thought I would have liked to design costumes, working with all those different fabrics—velvets and silks and brocades. Did you know that real silk is spun by caterpillars? It's fascinating. I read a whole book about the Silk Road once. But yes, those nights with the motor running, I just keep moving and moving from one project to the next.\n\nDoctor: During those nights when you have all that energy and keep moving from project to project, how is your mood? Do you feel particularly happy, excited, or on top of the world—or does your mood feel more normal, or perhaps irritable or down?\n\nPatient: Oh, my mood... well, on those days, I feel absolutely radiant. Like I've been chosen for something magnificent, you know? \"Radiant\" is such a wonderful word. It makes me think of radium. Did you know they used to paint watch dials with radium so they would glow in the dark? The poor girls who painted them, the Radium Girls, they would lick their brushes to get a fine point. Just a terrible tragedy. I used to have a beautiful vintage watch with a mother-of-pearl face, though it wasn't radium, thank goodness. My father bought it for me in Switzerland. Switzerland is breathtaking in the spring. The Alps just pierce the sky, and the air is so crisp. I always wanted to go back and take the Glacier Express train. \n\nBut yes, radiant and chosen. I used to love the smell of chalk dust in elementary school... the teacher would ask me to take the erasers outside and clap them together against the brick wall. Such a satisfying puff of white dust. But yes, it's infuriating when they try to erase me like that.\n\nDoctor: Besides these times when you feel radiant and energetic with the voices, have you had extended periods—lasting weeks or longer—where you felt depressed, sad, or hopeless, even if the voices weren't happening or seemed quieter?\n\nPatient: Well, depressed... yes, I suppose you could say that. There are these long, long stretches where I just sit at my kitchen table. I have these little terracotta pots of herbs on the windowsill—basil, thyme, a lovely rosemary bush. But during those times, I just sit there and watch them dry out. I don't water them, I don't pinch off the dead leaves. I just sit. Terracotta is such a fascinating material, isn't it? \"Baked earth\" in Italian. The ancient Romans used it for everything, even their plumbing pipes. I read somewhere that the Roman aqueducts were an absolute marvel of engineering. They moved water across entire valleys using just gravity. Gravity is a strange thing to think about. Sitting out on a summer evening with a glass of lemonade... \n\nBut yes, even during those perfectly normal weeks, the whispering was still there, and the phone was definitely being monitored.\n\nDoctor: When you think back to those several weeks when you felt completely normal—not energized, not depressed, just regular—and you were still hearing the women's voices whispering about the photographs: did those voices feel like they were part of your own mind, or did they feel like they were coming from outside you, from an external source like the walls or other people?\n\nPatient: Well, they definitely aren't my own thoughts. No, they're coming from outside. Like I said, I keep hearing these clear voices in my apartment, like women whispering right from behind the walls, telling me which photographs belong in the archive. And sometimes I hear them when I'm out, too, in empty museum rooms. \n\nMuseum walls are so thick, usually. They have to be, to regulate the temperature and humidity for the art. Climate control is absolutely vital for preserving photographs and paintings. If it gets too humid, you get foxing—those little brown spots on old paper. It's actually a type of fungus, did you know that? Fungi are incredible organisms. They aren't plants, and they aren't animals. They have their own entire kingdom. The largest living organism on earth is actually a fungus in Oregon. A honey fungus, they call it. It covers thousands of acres underground, just this massive network of mycelium. It makes you wonder what else is growing right beneath our feet, completely out of sight. Like truffles! People use pigs or dogs to sniff out truffles because they grow entirely underground. I've always loved dogs. A good Golden Retriever is worth their weight in gold, just like the name says. They have such gentle mouths they can carry a raw egg without breaking it. But yes, the voices... they definitely come from the walls, outside of me. Not from my own mind at all.\n\nDoctor: During those several weeks when you felt completely normal and still heard the voices—did that normal period last for at least two weeks or longer without you feeling radiant and energized at any point during it?\n\nPatient: Yes, oh absolutely. It was a period of several weeks, definitely longer than two. During that whole stretch, I wasn't especially energized or grand at all. Just... regular, like I said. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment the entire time, and I remained entirely convinced that the arts people were monitoring my phone. \n\nTelephones are so easy to tap, you know. It makes you think about how the old switchboard operators used to be able to just listen in on anyone's conversation if they wanted to. My great-aunt Mildred was a switchboard operator back in the 1940s. She had to sit in this cramped room for hours, just plugging those heavy cords into the giant board, connecting calls all across the city. It must have been exhausting, staring at those little flashing lights all day. Lights are fascinating, aren't they? Everyone always gives Thomas Edison all the credit for the lightbulb, but Nikola Tesla was the real visionary. Alternating current! It powers the entire modern world. Have you ever seen a Tesla coil in person, doctor? They shoot actual purple lightning right into the air. \n\nOf course, lightning is really just a massive discharge of static electricity. When I was little, I used to shuffle my feet on the wool rug in our living room during the winter, just so I could sneak up and shock my older brother on the ear. Wool is incredible for static. And it keeps you so warm because of the natural lanolin. Did you know New Zealand has more sheep than people? It sounds like such a peaceful place to live, just rolling green hills and sheep grazing everywhere. I've always wanted to visit the fjords there... \n\nBut yes, to answer your question, it was a good several weeks of no grand energy whatsoever, just regular, but the whispering and the phone monitoring were still happening.\n\nDoctor: During those several weeks when you felt completely normal and heard the whispers about the photographs—if someone had asked you at that time whether you believed the arts people were actually monitoring your phone, would you have said yes with complete certainty, or would you have had some doubt about whether it was really happening?\n\nPatient: Well, I would have said yes with absolute certainty. I still say yes with absolute certainty. I mean, I am completely convinced the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. They know my Caribbean archive will change how the galleries tell the truth, and no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise. Not a single person has given me a shred of evidence to the contrary. \n\nEvidence is so tricky, though, isn't it? In a court of law, they talk about \"beyond a reasonable doubt,\" but what is reasonable, really? Juries have such a hard job. Twelve angry men, right? Henry Fonda was brilliant in that movie. He had such a calm demeanor. My father loved Henry Fonda. We used to watch old black-and-white movies on Sunday afternoons. They had this big, heavy Zenith television set in a wooden cabinet. It took a full minute just to warm up the tubes before the picture would appear. Vacuum tubes! They used to run early computers on those, before transistors. ENIAC, I think it was called, took up an entire room just to do basic math. Now people walk around with tiny computers in their pockets, pretending they're just phones. But they aren't just phones, are they? They're tracking devices. Everyone willingly carrying around a little tracking device. It's exactly like George Orwell predicted in 1984, only we bought the screens ourselves. Big Brother doesn't even have to force us. \n\nBut yes, doctor, I was and still am completely certain about the arts people monitoring my phone. There's no doubt in my mind at all.\n\nDoctor: Looking back at those several weeks when you felt completely normal—not energized, not depressed—and you were hearing the whispers and convinced about the phone monitoring: did that normal period happen at a time when you were NOT having any of those very energetic nights where you felt radiant and chosen?\n\nPatient: Yes, exactly. Like I was saying before, there was a period of several weeks when I wasn't having any of those radiant nights. I wasn't energized, I wasn't feeling grand or chosen or anything like that. Just regular. But I still heard the whispers in the apartment, and I was still completely convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone. \n\nIt's funny how time works like that, isn't it? Weeks can just slip by. My grandmother used to say that time goes faster the older you get because each year is a smaller percentage of your life. Mathematically, it makes perfect sense. Mathematics is the universal language, really. If we ever make contact with extraterrestrials, we won't use English or Mandarin to speak to them, we'll use prime numbers. Carl Sagan talked about that. He helped put together the Golden Record that went up on the Voyager spacecraft. It has music on it—Bach, Beethoven, Chuck Berry. Can you imagine some alien civilization millions of years from now finding a gold-plated record and trying to figure out how to play it? They'd have to build a turntable from scratch just to hear \"Johnny B. Goode.\" \n\nMusic is so mathematical, though. The intervals, the frequencies. Pythagoras figured that out in ancient Greece. He thought the whole universe was made of numbers and harmonies. The \"music of the spheres,\" he called it. He believed the planets literally made a humming sound as they moved through space. Space is supposed to be a vacuum, though, so sound shouldn't be able to travel. But who knows what we'll discover next? The James Webb telescope is seeing galaxies from the very beginning of time now. \n\nBut yes, to answer your question, during those several weeks, I wasn't having any of those highly energetic, radiant nights at all. I was just regular, but the whispers and the phone tapping were still happening.\n\nDoctor: When you were feeling radiant and energized, were the whispers about the photographs telling you to do things that matched that grand, chosen feeling—like they were helping you with your important archive work? Or were the whispers saying the same things regardless of whether you felt radiant or just regular?\n\nPatient: Well, during the periods when I was sleeping only a few hours and just racing from one archive task to another, I was also hearing the women’s voices. And I was feeling absolutely certain the museum board was tracking my work then, too. So it was all happening even when I was so busy and energized. \n\nThe archiving work is just so delicate, you know. You have to use acid-free folders for absolutely everything. Did you know that most books printed after 1850 are literally destroying themselves? They switched to wood pulp paper and added rosin sizing, which actually creates sulfuric acid over time. The pages just turn yellow and crumble into dust right on the shelf. It’s a tragedy, really, losing all that history. Before that, they made paper out of old cotton and linen rags, and rag paper lasts for centuries! People used to sell their worn-out clothes to the rag-and-bone man. Such a strange job, walking the streets of London or New York calling out for old rags and bones. They used the bones for all sorts of things, actually—fertilizer, buttons, knife handles. \n\nMy grandfather had a pocket knife with a bone handle. It was so smooth from years of him holding it. He used to sit on the back porch and peel apples with it, all in one long, continuous ribbon of skin. He was so precise. He told me once that if you threw the apple peel over your shoulder, it would land on the ground and form the initial of the person you were going to marry. It always just looked like a curly 'S' or a 'C' to me, no matter how I threw it. Apples are so wonderful in the fall, though. We used to go picking up in upstate New York, Macintosh and Honeycrisp... the cider they made there was just incredible, they pressed it right in this big wooden barn...\n\nDoctor: During those several weeks when you felt completely normal—not energized, not depressed, just regular—and you were still hearing the whispers and convinced about the phone monitoring: did you feel like your thinking was clear and logical during those weeks, or did your thoughts feel confused or disorganized in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, I always feel like my thinking is perfectly logical, but I suppose it doesn't always come out that way to other people, even when my mood is just regular. Like, my cousin will call and ask me a very simple question, just about a utility bill or an upcoming appointment, and I try to answer her. But I'll start explaining the archive grant, and then that leads into the historical Caribbean shipping routes, and then I'll get into talking about my grandmother’s altar, and by the time I finally stop talking, nobody seems to know what I meant at all. She just gets so confused. \n\nThe shipping routes really are fascinating, though. The trade winds just naturally carry the vessels across the Atlantic. The ocean currents are like invisible highways in the water. Water is so incredibly powerful, isn't it? It carves out entire canyons over millions of years. When I was a little girl, I used to love walking along the beach collecting sea glass. You'd find these beautiful, frosted pieces of green and blue glass that used to be medicine bottles or soda bottles. They say it takes decades for the sand and the waves to tumble a sharp piece of broken glass into something that smooth. We used to put them in a clear mason jar on the kitchen windowsill so the morning sun would shine right through them. \n\nMy mother had this gorgeous stained glass lamp in the parlor, too. It was a Tiffany style, with these intricate green dragonflies all around the shade. Dragonflies are actually incredible creatures, you know. They can fly backwards and hover in mid-air like tiny little helicopters. I read once that they catch their prey with almost a ninety-five percent success rate, which is better than lions or sharks or anything else in the animal kingdom. Nature is just perfectly designed that way... \n\nBut I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, my thoughts. Yes, even during those quiet weeks, my cousin would ask about a simple bill and I'd just lose her completely with everything else going on in my head.\n\nDoctor: When you think back over these eight months, can you tell me roughly how many weeks total you were feeling radiant and energized with all that extra energy—add those up together—and then roughly how many weeks total you were sitting at the kitchen table feeling drained and hopeless?\n\nPatient: Well, if I try to add it all up... most of these months since my retirement have really been dominated by those stretches of feeling completely driven and chosen. I was just so irritable and completely unable to slow down. Even when I was having some of those quieter, withdrawn days sitting at the table, the energized periods just took over most of the time. \n\nRetirement is such a strange transition, anyway. They gave me this lovely mantel clock when I left. It has a heavy brass pendulum that swings back and forth. Pendulums are actually fascinating, you know. Galileo figured out the principle of the pendulum by watching a bronze chandelier swing back and forth during a church service in Pisa. He used his own pulse to time how long each swing took. It’s incredible to think about using your own heartbeat as a stopwatch. The human heart beats something like a hundred thousand times a day. It’s the most hardworking muscle we have. \n\nI used to be very conscious of my heart rate back in the eighties when I took step aerobics classes. Oh, everyone was doing it back then, wearing those bright neon leotards and the thick scrunchy socks over our leggings. Jane Fonda really started a whole revolution with those workout tapes. My friend Susan and I would do the tapes in her living room, and her orange tabby cat would always try to attack our shoelaces while we were doing grapevines across the carpet. Cats are so funny about sudden movements. They have that predator instinct just hardwired into them from their wild ancestors in the desert... \n\nBut yes, what was the question? Oh, the weeks. It was mostly those driven, chosen stretches dominating everything since I retired, with just some of those drained, withdrawn days mixed in here and there.\n\nDoctor: When you first started hearing those women's voices eight months ago, did the voices begin during one of those energetic, radiant periods, or did they start during a time when your mood was completely normal and regular?\n\nPatient: Well, when they first started eight months ago, my mood was actually just completely regular. There was a period of several weeks right at the beginning when I was not especially energized or grand at all, but I still heard the whispers in the apartment and I remained absolutely convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone. \n\nTelephones are just so invasive now, aren't they? You know, when I was growing up, we only had one phone in the whole house, and it was attached to the kitchen wall with a long, coiled cord. It was a harvest gold rotary phone. You had to stick your finger in the little holes and pull the dial all the way around. If you were calling someone with a lot of eights and nines in their number, it took forever! And that cord, it would get so twisted up over time. My mother used to stretch it all the way into the dining room so she could smoke a cigarette and talk to her sister in private. Smoking was everywhere back then. People even smoked on airplanes and in hospitals! Can you imagine? The flight attendants used to walk down the aisles handing out little packets of cigarettes with the airline logo on them. Flying used to be such an elegant experience. People would dress up in their Sunday best just to get on a plane. The stewardesses wore those beautiful tailored uniforms, sometimes designed by famous couturiers like Emilio Pucci. He used such bold, geometric prints and bright colors. Fashion in the sixties was really just a massive explosion of color and freedom after the strictness of the fifties... \n\nOh, I'm sorry, I drifted off again. But yes, to answer your question, when it all first began eight months ago, I wasn't energized. It was a stretch of several weeks where I felt completely normal, but the whispers and the phone monitoring were already happening.\n\nDoctor: Looking back over these eight months, have there been any days or weeks where you felt completely normal—not energized, not depressed, just regular—and during those normal periods, you did NOT hear the women's voices whispering about the photographs at all?\n\nPatient: No, not a single day. The voices and the absolute certainty that people are watching my archive have been present for about eight months now, straight through. Even on the days when my mood is just perfectly regular and quiet, they're still there whispering. \n\nEight months is a long time to be watched, you know. You mentioned the photographs, and it actually makes me think of how I used to shoot on this beautiful old Leica camera. It belonged to my father. Film photography is really a lost art now with all these digital phones. You had to be so careful with the exposure and the light meters. And the darkroom! The smell of the developer fluid, the stop bath, the fixer... it was like pure alchemy. You'd just stand there under that red safelight and watch the image magically appear on the paper while it was submerged in the tray. \n\nWe used to hang the wet prints up on a little indoor clothesline with wooden clothespins to dry. Clothespins are such a simple, perfect invention, aren't they? I think the Shakers invented the spring-loaded ones. Or maybe they just perfected them. The Shakers made such beautiful, simple things. Those ladder-back chairs! They would hang the chairs right on the walls on wooden pegs when they weren't using them, just to keep the floors clear for sweeping. Sweeping is actually very meditative. Monks do it in monasteries just to clear the mind. A good broom made of real broomcorn is getting so hard to find these days, everything is just cheap plastic...\n\nBut I'm sorry, I lost the thread again. What did you ask? Oh, right, if they ever stopped. No, they haven't. The voices and the watching, it's been a solid eight months of it, without any break at all."
